title: Wounded healers
hook: our wounds, healed, can help others

segments.voice: Yesterday: the beam in your own eye, and Paul's all have sinned. Your line was all of us.

A church basement on a weeknight. A steel coffee urn, a box of tissues passed hand to hand. The person who runs the group doesn't have a degree in anything. What she has is a memory: years ago she sat in that same room, shaking, and somebody who'd been there before her stayed until the end of the night. Now she's the one who stays. There's a name for people like her. Henri Nouwen, a Catholic priest and writer, used it as the title of a book.

Paul opens his second letter to Corinth praising God "who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God." Read it slowly and it's a relay. The comfort you were handed is the comfort you hand on. And Paul isn't writing from a comfortable chair. A few lines later he says they were "pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life." The healer is still limping. Then Isaiah's servant song, met in year two, which Christians read about Jesus: "with his stripes we are healed." Stripes: the marks left by blows. Here, healing comes through wounds, not around them. Then Luke. The risen Jesus stands among his frightened friends, who think they are seeing a spirit, and he says, "Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself." Luke doesn't describe the marks; John's Gospel does, with the print of the nails. But in Luke the hands and feet that went to the cross are how his friends know him. So a healed wound isn't one that never happened. It's one that closed and left a mark that can be shown. That doesn't mean every hurt has to be put to work right away. A wound that's still bleeding needs care first, and nobody owes anyone their story. But the ones that have closed can become a map for someone still lost in the same country.

Go back to one wound that has mostly healed, a loss, a failure, an illness, a hard year; not the one that's still raw, which can stay in care for now. Notice what got you through, a person, a sentence somebody said, a small kindness, and ask who is standing in that place now; if you pray, ask how your scar might help them. If an old wound ever opens into thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Wounded healers. People whose healed hurts help them help others, the way Paul says comfort received becomes comfort given.
Your line: wounds that heal. Comfort received becomes comfort given. Go gently.

howItsDone: Some Christians serve others through what they have suffered: in grief groups, recovery groups, hospital visiting and prison ministry, people who have walked through something offer their company to those who are walking through it now.

chat.says: I went through something awful years ago. Could that ever actually help somebody?
options: Paul says the comfort we receive is what we hand on. A closed wound can become a map.
Only if you tell your whole story to everyone, even while it still hurts.
Paul says real helpers are people who were never hurt, so they stay steady.
chat.meaning: Paul says God comforts us so we can comfort others with that same comfort. Wounds that have closed can help; raw ones need care first.

notes: Henri Nouwen named as a Catholic priest and writer who used 'The Wounded Healer' as a book title; no quotation. Confirm.
2 Corinthians 1:4 KJV begins 'Who comforteth us'; the lesson lowercases 'who' mid-sentence. Confirm acceptable.
Isaiah 53 read as about Jesus is a Christian reading; Jewish readers understand the servant differently. The lesson says 'which Christians read about Jesus'.
'Stripes, as in the marks of a whip' is an explanatory gloss; confirm.
Original: παράκλησις and its verb recur in 2 Corinthians 1:3–7; confirm the note.

Audit: Luke 24:39–40 shows hands and feet but never mentions wounds or scars; the teach, screen head, myth, fork reveal and trapdoor no longer say 'in Luke the risen Jesus keeps his scars', and credit the nail prints to John 20:25–27.
